description.text: Heinrich Mann was born on 27 March 1871 in Lübeck, the eldest son of a grain merchant and senator. From an early age he cultivated a sharp, satirical voice that would later make him a leading critic of the rising tide of fascism in Germany. His novels, especially the scathing satire *Der Untertan*, earned him both acclaim and notoriety during the Weimar Republic, but his outspoken opposition to the Nazis forced him to flee the country in 1933.

After a brief exile in France, Mann escaped to the United States with the help of the American journalist Varian Fry. In exile he continued to write, producing works such as *Die Jugend des Königs Henri Quatre*, while his relationship with his more famous brother Thomas remained strained. Mann died in Santa Monica on 11 March 1950, leaving behind a legacy of political engagement and literary criticism that continues to be studied.

curiosities.text: Mann’s novel *Professor Unrat* was adapted into the 1930 film *The Blue Angel*, in which Marlene Dietrich made her first sound‑film appearance and launched her international career.

During the German occupation of France, Mann and a group of exiles—including his wife Nelly and friends Alma Mahler-Werfel and Franz Werfel—hiked for six hours to cross the border at Port Bou, eventually reaching Portugal and boarding the S.S. Nea Hellas to New York.
